title: Stacking Context and Top-Layer Behavior
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of Stacking Context and Top-Layer Behavior and recognize when it is useful.
Apply a relevant property, selector, or technique from this lesson in a small stylesheet.
Inspect the browser result and explain one behavior, limitation, or compatibility consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore Stacking Context and Top-Layer Behavior through a small CSS example, a visual guide, and one practical check. You do not need to memorize every property at once; focus on the decision the browser is making.
content.why_it_matters: Stacking Context and Top-Layer Behavior helps you build interfaces that remain understandable, maintainable, and usable as content and viewport conditions change.

content_blocks.title: Positioning and stacking contexts
content_blocks.alt_text: Positioning finds a containing block; stacking contexts control which groups can layer. Labels show the concept flow.
content_blocks.caption: Use the labeled steps as a reasoning guide; detailed behavior is described in the lesson.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Positioning changes how a box is placed relative to its containing block or viewport. Layering also depends on stacking contexts, so a larger `z-index` does not always escape a parent context.

content_blocks.title: A useful way to practice
content_blocks.text: Start with one element or component. Use the concepts in this lesson—properties that create stacking contexts, positioned elements and transforms, isolation and compositing—and change one declaration at a time. Compare the page before and after the change.

items.title: Properties that create stacking contexts
items.text: Keep text legible at default and zoomed sizes; allow long words and translated content to wrap without hiding information.

items.title: Positioned elements and transforms
items.text: Keep motion nonessential, honor reduced-motion preferences, and inspect performance on a real device when practical.

items.title: Isolation and compositing
items.text: Connect isolation and compositing to the main idea in stacking context and top-layer behavior, then verify it in a minimal browser example.

items.title: The browser top layer
items.text: Compare the declarations in cascade order instead of assuming that the longest selector or last file always wins.

items.title: Backdrops and layered interfaces

content_blocks.expected_output: The badge is positioned inside the card’s containing block; inset properties adapt to writing direction.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original CSS snippet, save the file, and repeat the test. Remove temporary debugging rules before keeping a final version.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Inspect the actual winning declaration and solve the cause before adding a new override or !important.

content.task: Try it yourself: build a small example that demonstrates Stacking Context and Top-Layer Behavior. Use the simplest relevant selector and one or more declarations, inspect the browser result, and explain it in your own words.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to connect a visual change to its cause.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one property, save, and compare again.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the last rule always wins.
common_mistakes.why: The cascade also considers origin, importance, layers and selector specificity; scope and source order may also matter.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect matched declarations and computed styles before changing the stylesheet.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only one viewport or interaction state.
common_mistakes.why: A rule can work at one width and fail when content, focus, zoom or preferences change.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat the check at narrow and wide widths and include keyboard focus or reduced-motion checks when relevant.
